facts.text: San Francisco is suing the Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company behind Truth Social, for selling early access to President Donald Trump’s posts on the social media site.
Trump Media hasn’t disclosed its list of Truth API clients, but the company has said it plans on marketing the product to AI companies and large news organizations.
On August 21st, for example, Trump posted that the federal government was going to “lower the price of ground beef for working families” by exempting some ground beef imports from tariffs.
“In today’s markets, early access means millions of dollars.
This isn’t the first time Trump has been sued over Truth API.

President Donald Trump's media company says it plans to launch a new service that would let paying customers see certain Truth Social posts milliseconds before other users, including posts that could affect financial markets or national security.
The service, called Truth PSI, was announced Thursday by Trump Media & Technology Group.
Shares of Trump Media rose 0.6% Thursday to $9.63.

Critics raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest. “He’s selling expedited, privileged access to information about what he is doing as president,” said Kathleen Clark, a Washington University School of Law professor who studies government conflicts of interest. “It’s yet more brazen corruption, an improper exploitation of government power to enrich himself.” The company says Truth PSI is part of a broader effort to generate new revenue.
The company also did not say whether President Trump's posts would be included.

The early access service comes as the publicly traded Trump Media loses hundreds of millions of dollars each quarter and its stock has dropped below $10 from $62 shortly after going public two years ago.

Trump is the largest shareholder of Trump Media, owning more than 40% of its shares through a trust.
The new subscription service rolled out earlier this month is charging Wall Street firms as much as $100,000 a month to trade off the market-moving posts before others.

“A president selling priority access to news he himself generates for the benefit of a private company he controls is so blatantly corrupt and unconstitutional that it would have been hard to even fathom just a few years ago,” said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, a plaintiff in the case along with news outlet The Intercept.
